explain.say: Have you ever pushed a buggy, pulled a suitcase or ridden a bike up a little slope at the edge of the pavement? That slope was built for wheelchair users, but you used it too! Look at the board. Accessibility means designing places and things so everyone can use them.

explain.say: See the first group, moving around? Ramps, lifts, wide doors and low kerbs help people who use wheelchairs or walking sticks. They also help parents with prams and delivery workers with trolleys. Where have you seen a ramp?

explain.say: Now look at seeing. Braille is raised dots that blind people read with their fingers. Tactile paving is bumpy tiles on train platforms that you can feel with your feet or a cane. Large print and audio description help too. Have you ever felt bumpy tiles at a station?

faq.a: Accessibility means designing buildings, transport, websites and products so that everyone, including disabled people, can use them easily and with dignity.

faq.q: How do ramps and lifts help?
faq.a: They let people who use wheelchairs, walkers or crutches move between levels without stairs. They also help parents with prams, older people and anyone carrying heavy things.
Braille is a reading system of raised dots that blind and partially sighted people read with their fingertips. It was invented by Louis Braille in France, who was blind himself, in the 1820s.

faq.q: How do captions help deaf people?
faq.a: Captions show spoken words and important sounds as text on screen, so deaf and hard of hearing people can follow videos, films and live events.
It is when something designed for disabled people helps almost everyone. Lowered kerbs for wheelchairs also help prams, bikes and suitcases; captions help people in noisy places.

facts: Louis Braille published his raised-dot reading system in 1829, when he was about 20.
Tactile paving was invented by Seiichi Miyake and first laid in Okayama, Japan, in 1967.

quiz.say: Which of these helps a blind person find the edge of a train platform?
quiz.show: Which helps a blind person at a platform edge?
quiz.why: Tactile paving has bumps you can feel with your feet or a cane, warning of the edge.

wrong.0: Captions help with hearing, not finding edges.
wrong.2: A hearing loop helps people with hearing aids.

quiz.say: A lowered kerb built for wheelchairs also helps a parent with a pram. What is this called?
quiz.why: The curb-cut effect is when design for disabled people helps almost everyone.

wrong.1: The bandwagon effect is about copying what is popular.
wrong.2: The medical model is a way of thinking about disability, not a design effect.
